passage:
Monday: Harish and Ojas argued over whose turn it was on the carrom board at the society clubhouse. It ended in a sulk.
Tuesday: The argument started again at the bus stop, with six kids from their building watching. Ojas said Harish cheated. Harish felt every eye on him, and his chest went tight. "At least I didn't cry on sports day in Class 2 like you," he said, loudly. Someone laughed. "And your dad's scooter sounds like a sick goat." More laughter. Harish didn't care about carrom anymore; he only needed to win.
Friday: Ojas sat at the far end of the bus. Harish kept looking at the back of his head. The laughter from Tuesday didn't feel so good now.

qa.q: Where did the second argument happen, and who was watching?
qa.a: It happened at the bus stop, with six kids from their building watching.

qa.q: Why did Harish bring up Ojas's dad and sports day at the bus stop?
qa.a: With every eye on him he felt cornered, so winning mattered more than the carrom game and he picked words meant to hurt.

qa.q: What could have stopped the stakes rising at the bus stop?
qa.a: Harish could have noticed his tight chest and said "Let's sort it later", or an older kid could have split them up before the crowd made it a show.

qa.q: What is it like for Ojas by Friday?
qa.a: Ojas seems hurt and wants distance, sitting at the far end of the bus after being laughed at about his dad in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a child, cornered in front of onlookers, dragging in an old embarrassment and mocking a friend's family just to win.

passage: Sit, Vikas. You think your Dadi never fought? When I was nine, Sunaina and I quarrelled over a skipping rope in the lane behind the mill. Other girls gathered round, and that crowd made me feel trapped. I had to win. So I dug up old things: how she had copied my sums in Class 3, how her frocks were always hand-me-downs from her cousins. The girls went "Oooh." Sunaina's face crumpled and she ran home. I stood there with the rope, feeling like a queen for one minute. Then the lane was empty, and the rope was just a rope. It took us a whole summer to talk properly again. That is why I stopped you today, beta, when you started on your friend's mother.

qa.q: What were Dadi and Sunaina quarrelling over?
qa.a: They quarrelled over a skipping rope in the lane behind the mill.

qa.q: How did the crowd of girls make young Dadi feel?
qa.a: The crowd made her feel trapped, so she felt she had to win, even by saying things meant to hurt Sunaina.

qa.q: What could young Dadi have done when she felt trapped by the crowd?
qa.a: She could have said she didn't want to fight in front of everyone and walked away, then talked to Sunaina alone later about the rope.

qa.q: How was Sunaina affected when the old things were brought up?
qa.a: Sunaina was hurt and shamed in front of the other girls; her face crumpled and she ran home, and it took a whole summer to mend.

grounding: Shows a child who, feeling trapped by an audience, digs up old grievances and mocks a friend's clothes and family to win.
